title: How I got AI to make 370 animated prehistoric creatures for my evolution RTS (and why the walk cycles had to be rigged in code)
author: Deep_Time2027
selftext:
So just for context, before this I had done a summer camp as a kid to make video game, a coding class in high school, and making some moderately successful mods for my favorite strategy games. I heard about "vibe-coding" and was immediately intrigued since I loved designing my mods, but no longer have the time to actually work on them, so being able to straight up create games without having to spend hours on the manual work of it all sounded incredible. I signed up for Claude with a game idea I have had for a long time, but I lacked the skills/resources/and time to ever attempt it. 

The result is "Deep Time", a strategy game where you steer evolution from the first animals to crawl onto land through 360 million years of Earth's history. It has 370+ real species, and each one has a 16-frame sprite sheet: walk, eat, attack and die. Here's how the art pipeline ended up working, including the parts that didn't.



1. Sheets from an image model. Initially this was super unreliable, I was using a free imiage model, and it could not keep a consistent art style. Eventually I tried Gemini and it worked great, from then on, each species now gets a prompt plus a style reference sheet, sent to Gemini. A sheet costs about $0.14 and takes 20–35 seconds. A script cuts each 4x4 grid into frames, keys out the magenta background, and a quality filter rejects or repairs bad frames.

![img](vb1g0b27vd3i1 "Tyrannosaurus before and after: left, the sheet the game used from Oct 25; right, the first Gemini-drawn sheet of Oct 31, when 101 species were redrawn in one painted style (backgrounds evened out here).")

2. Prompt lessons that actually mattered



\- Describe what it looks like, not what it isn't. "Never a modern crocodile" produced modern crocodiles twice. "A land predator with a box-shaped head" worked first time.

\- The model copies the reference. A fish in my reference sheet's eating frame turned up in almost every species' eating frame until I named each species' food.

\- Attaching an already-approved close relative's sheet fixed species that words alone couldn't.

\- Some animals never work. A gliding reptile with skin between its \*legs\* got the skin on its arms in 7 of 7 tries, so I cut it from the game.

![img](ke39a0ogvd3i1 "Sharovipteryx, attempts 2 and 6 of 7: the gliding skin always ended up on the arms, so the species was dropped.")



3. A review page. Every species plays its animations in a browser page where I mark problems: shuffle walk, curled tail, inconsistent frames, too smooth. I reviewed 221 species in one sitting and marked 125. My rule after that: if one frame is bad, mend that frame; never regenerate a sheet whose walk already works.

![img](xq5di3qrvd3i1)

4. Walk cycles: where image AI fails. Ask for a walk in any wording and you get one pose drawn four times, a shuffle. Painting real legs over stick-leg guides helped, but never reliably. What worked was rigging the AI's painted drawings in code: the legs cut out onto triangle meshes and bent by bones, posed into a step-pass-step cycle with a bobbing body. That covered about 50 species in two days: bird-like legs for theropods, column legs for sauropods, a bending wing mesh for a pterosaur. Swimmers move by build: fish-shaped reptiles sweep their tails side to side, whales beat theirs up and down, and flipper animals row with a still body.

![img](0zb3b63xvd3i1 "The stick-leg trick for walk cycles (Nov 7): near legs in white and far legs in grey drawn onto Tyrannosaurus' standing pose in the four steps of a walk (left), which Gemini then painted over (right). Asked for a walk directly, it drew one pose four times.")



![img](ek6fmvf3wd3i1 "Walk rigs (Nov 12): top, Dimetrodon's painted walk as it was, the legs barely moving (a 'shuffle'); bottom, the same painted drawing rigged in code on a bending mesh so its legs take real steps.")



Tools: Godot 4. Gemini for the sprite sheets. The code, rigging tools included, was written with Claude Code under my direction.



It's free on itch (Windows, Mac and browser; still in development, so expect bugs): [https://redeef.itch.io/deep-time](https://redeef.itch.io/deep-time)



Happy to answer questions about any part of the pipeline.
